newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Slowdown in UK sales soothes fears of boom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Slowdown in UK sales soothes fears of boom.

text.p: High street sales in Britain fell unexpectedly in December, official figures showed on Wednesday, confirming a disappointing Christmas for retailers and helping to allay fears of a runaway boom in consumer spending.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said retail sales fell 0.8 percent in December, following a 0.8 percent rise in November. Sales were 2.9 percent higher than in December 1995, down from November's 4.0 percent annual growth rate.

Economists said the data would help finance minister Kenneth Clarke to resist pressure from the Bank of England, which fears inflation is about to take off again, to increase interest rates and might enable him to hold rates steady until after the looming election.

The Conservative government, which has made Britain's economic health the central issue in its election campaign, welcomed the data, saying the underlying trend was of healthy growth in retail sales and expanding consumer spending.

Economists said the slowdown in sales suggested thrifty British consumers did not indulge in lavish Christmas spending as expected and were still reluctant to pay higher prices, despite growing confidence and job security.
"These data suggest that the consumer is still not prepared to accept significant prices increases," said Bank of America economist Jeremy Hawkins.
"This argues against any marked deterioration in the inflation outlook even if, as seems likely, the December slide in sales proves just a temporary phenomenon."
Economists said Clarke, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, would pounce on the data to ward off increasingly public calls from the Bank of England to raise interest rates from the present 6.0 percent.

Clarke, who has the final say on monetary policy after hearing advice from Bank of England Governor Eddie George, is reluctant to raise rates before the election because this would mean dearer mortgages for millions of home-owners.
An election must be held by May 22 and the opposition Labour party has a commanding lead in opinion polls.

In an unusually forthright speech on Monday night, George urged Clarke raise interest rates immediately and said he should not use the strength of the pound, which reduces the cost of imported goods, as an excuse for delaying action.
"The trend in retail sales is still reasonably firm," said Yamaichi chief economist John Shepperd.

"But if the Chancellor is looking for excuses not to put rates up before the election, then the recent accumulation of data has gone very much his way and this is another strong piece of ammunition for him in arguing against a rate rise."

The recent pick-up in retail sales, coupled with rising house prices and falling unemployment, had sparked some fears of a return to the runaway growth of the 1980s. But economists said December's sales data finally dispelled these fears.
"The data offer another piece of evidence, the strongest yet, that the froth has come off consumer demand," said Nikko economist Simon Briscoe.

The retail sales data mirrored evidence from recent surveys which pointed to slowing demand for clothing and footwear -- a sector which has seen sharp price rises in the past. That sector saw a 4.6 percent monthly drop in turnover in December.
"Consumers have punished retailers for recent price hikes in this area. At least some of these price rises could be reversed in coming months," said Dharshini David, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
